transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2025-09-14
Time: 09:30 PT / 16:30 UTC
Duration: ~55 minutes
Attendees: Anika Patel (Redwood AE), Marcus Lee (Redwood SE), Sofia Martinez (Keystone Lead Dev), Tom Chen (Keystone Platform Eng), Lydia Park (Keystone Security), Evan Brooks (Keystone DevOps)

Summary (auto): quick SDK integration walkthrough, environment + auth options, runbook to move from sandbox to prod, security checklist and next steps.

[00:00] Anika Patel: Alright, hi everyone, thanks for joining. I'm Anika from Redwood, and with me is Marcus, our SE. How's everyone doing?

[00:08] Sofia Martinez: Good, thanks. We've got a short agenda — mostly want to get the Python and TypeScript quickstarts running in our sandbox and chat about how keys and KMS would work.

[00:15] Marcus Lee: Awesome. We'll do a short live demo in the console then a live run of the SDK quickstart in both Python and TS, and then go through a deploy runbook and security concerns.

[02:10] Tom Chen: Quick callout, we have an internal requirement for key rotation and audit logs — also prefer VPC peering for dedicated deployments.

[02:25] Marcus Lee: Totally, we can cover VPC/Dedicated vs hosted and the Private offering. For rotation, Redwood supports KMS integrations and automated rotation workflows; we'll show the patterns.

[03:05] Lydia Park: Do you have example policies for RBAC and SSO/SAML?

[03:12] Anika Patel: Yes, we'll attach the security pack after the call. It includes SSO SAML setup, RBAC examples, and audit log retention options.

[03:40] Marcus Lee: Ok jumping into the console — note, I'm on a demo tenant so you'll see things labeled Demo-Org. Here's the API keys page, you can create scoped keys per environment, and tag them. For CI we recommend creating a minimal-scope service key and storing in your secret manager.

[04:15] Marcus Lee: (screen) I'll switch to the SDK quickstart docs -> python. The snippet looks like:

# python example in transcript (spoken)
from redwood import RedwoodClient
client = RedwoodClient(api_key=os.environ.get('REDWOOD_KEY'))
resp = client.generate('Write a one-sentence summary of the meeting')
print(resp.text)

[05:20] Sofia Martinez: That looks straightforward. For TypeScript?

[05:25] Marcus Lee: TS is basically the same. Spoken snippet:

// typescript (node)
import { Redwood } from '@redwoodai/sdk'
const client = new Redwood({ apiKey: process.env.REDWOOD_KEY })
const resp = await client.generate({ prompt: 'Summarize this meeting in one sentence' })
console.log(resp.text)

[06:10] Evan Brooks: Do you recommend storing the key in GitHub secrets or vault?

[06:15] Marcus Lee: We recommend HashiCorp Vault or cloud KMS-backed secret manager for production; GitHub Actions secrets are fine for CI short-lived, but rotate often. We have a sample workflow.

[07:05] Anika Patel: We'll paste Marcus's example GitHub Actions snippet into the notes — it's also in the repo we share.

[08:00] Marcus Lee: One gotcha — when you use prefix caching or long sessions, watch your KV cache sizing; it's in the Optimize console. Sorry, I said KV cache — sometimes the auto-transcript shows KV cash.

[08:30] Tom Chen: Can you explain the difference between using Hosted vs Dedicated for us? We want predictable latency for our realtime features.

[08:40] Marcus Lee: Yes. Hosted is fastest to get started — pay-as-you-go, good for lower predictability. Dedicated gives you reserved GPU pools, predictable p99 latency and throughput. Private (VPC) lets you run in your cloud with our control plane. For realtime p99 you probably want dedicated or private depending on compliance.

[09:55] Lydia Park: In private deployments do we still get the same console and rollouts?

[10:03] Marcus Lee: Yes, same console and APIs. The agent will connect to your VPC and we surface the same model catalog and rollouts. Some naming in the transcript earlier might get mangled — red wood vs Redwood — but it's the same.

[11:20] Marcus Lee: Now quick demo of a local run — I'll run the Python quickstart using a sandbox key. (typing sounds)

[11:40] Marcus Lee: The command is pip install redwood-sdk then export REDWOOD_KEY=... then python examples/quickstart.py. You should see a streaming response; in the SDK we surface a streaming iterator for tokens.

[13:10] Sofia Martinez: Is the streaming interface compatible with our current websocket layer?

[13:18] Marcus Lee: Yes, you can adapt — we return token chunks; you can pipe them to a websocket. There's a snippet in TypeScript exploring token streaming.

[15:00] Anika Patel: Let's pause and talk about secrets and KMS integrations. Marcus, can you run through KMS rotation?

[15:10] Marcus Lee: Sure. We support AWS KMS, GCP KMS and Azure Key Vault. Pattern we recommend: use a service principal / service account that has decrypt-only on the key; rotate your underlying key in KMS, then update the Redwood service key via our API or Console. We also support envelope encryption if you need double-wrap.

[16:00] Lydia Park: Do you provide an HSM option?

[16:05] Marcus Lee: For Private deployments yes, you can integrate with customer HSMs. For Hosted we integrate with cloud KMS. We'll include the HSM note in the security pack.

[17:20] Tom Chen: Request: example terraform or IAM policy so we can hand it to infra.

[17:28] Marcus Lee: Yep, action item — I'll send a terraform snippet for creating the role and key bindings.

[19:00] Evan Brooks: On the SDK side, we have multi-environment pipelines. What's the recommended runbook from sandbox to prod?

[19:10] Marcus Lee: Good question — typical runbook we recommend:
1) Sandbox: Use hosted with sample prompts and load tests.
2) Preprod: Move to Dedicated small pool or private sandbox, enable tracing and cost monitoring.
3) Pilot: Run internal traffic spike tests, enable prefix caching for frequently used prompts, set autoscaling policies.
4) Prod: Pin to specific model version, enable RBAC, enable KMS and rotate keys per policy, add canary rollout.

[21:00] Anika Patel: We'll attach a one-page runbook with exact CLI commands. Example CLI call in the notes: redwood models pin --model star-7b --env prod --duration 30d (spoken).

[22:40] Sofia Martinez: About observability — token-level billing, latency per route, is that visible in the console?

[22:48] Marcus Lee: Yes, per-route dashboards, token breakdown, and you can add tracing hooks to send spans to your APM. We'll share a dashboard export.

[24:10] Tom Chen: For our use, we will need audit logs sent to our SIEM. Is that supported?

[24:20] Marcus Lee: Yes, we can stream audit logs to your syslog or S3 with structured events. We'll include example event schema.

[25:30] Marcus Lee: Quick note on Optimize suggestions — for document ingestion workloads we often recommend int8 quantization profiles and medium batching. Optimize will suggest batch sizes based on observed latency distribution.

[27:00] Lydia Park: Any regulatory artifacts like SOC2, ISO?

[27:08] Anika Patel: Yes, we'll send the SOC2 attestation and ISO summary in the security pack. There is also a dataset handling doc for PII redaction patterns.

[28:40] Marcus Lee: Now a short live run of the TypeScript quickstart so you can see the set-up for streaming and function-calling. (typing) In our SDK we do function call hints — it will return structured JSON when you call tools.

[30:00] (short pause, background noise)

[30:12] Sofia Martinez: You mentioned function calling — can we limit functions per role?

[30:18] Marcus Lee: Yes, RBAC can restrict which service keys can call certain tool integrations. We'll include an example policy.

[32:00] Anika Patel: Let's go through the final checks for pilot: what do you need to feel comfortable?

[32:10] Sofia Martinez: We need security docs, a terraform/IAM snippet, and a small pilot estimate + costs. Also internal sign-off from security and ops.

[32:22] Anika Patel: Great. We'll provide those. For pilot sizing, Marcus, what's the typical minimum for a 3-week pilot?

[32:32] Marcus Lee: Usually a small dedicated pool equivalent to 1-2 GPUs or a hosted burst window depending on concurrency. We'll include both costed options.

[33:50] Tom Chen: Do you support multi-region fallbacks? We need a DR plan.

[33:58] Marcus Lee: Yes, smart routing will failover to a compatible model in another region. You can set routing policy by latency or cost. We'll include a diagram.

[35:12] Evan Brooks: If we go private, what's the network setup? Peering vs private link?

[35:20] Marcus Lee: We support VPC peering and PrivateLink equivalents; for on-prem there's an agent. We'll send the network runbook.

[36:40] Lydia Park: About data retention — how long are logs and payloads retained by default?

[36:47] Marcus Lee: By default hosted logs kept 30 days; for enterprise you can configure retention and bring-your-own-storage for longer retention. We'll document the defaults.

[38:00] Anika Patel: Ok last demo note — here's the example CI workflow Marcus mentioned: (spoken)

jobs:
  deploy:
    steps:
      - name: checkout
      - name: set REDWOOD_KEY
        uses: hashicorp/vault-action@v1
      - name: call redwood test
        run: node tests/generate.test.mjs

[40:20] Sofia Martinez: That fits our pipeline.

[41:00] Marcus Lee: Wrapping up with next steps: we'll send security pack, terraform + CI examples, pilot pricing and Dedicated sizing. Also we'll set up a follow-up 30-min kick-off for the pilot.

[42:10] Anika Patel: Any final questions?

[42:20] Lydia Park: One last — can you provide sample prompt sets for hallucination/regression tests?

[42:26] Marcus Lee: Yes, we have a prompt regression pack and eval harness. I'll share it.

[44:00] Sofia Martinez: Great, thank you. We'll review the materials and propose dates for the pilot.

[44:12] Anika Patel: Thanks all, we'll send the artifacts by EOD tomorrow.

[44:20] (meeting ends)

Notes on transcript quality: there are a few auto-transcription errors in product names and acronyms; speaker labels are accurate for the most part but some short crosstalk was condensed.
